'''Elizabeth A. Rauscher''' (March 18, 1937<ref name=":0">Elizabeth Valerie Ann Rauscher, PhD. [http://www.mykeeper.com/profile/ElizabethRauscher/ 1937-2019]</ref> – July 3, 2019) was an American [[physicist]] and [[parapsychologist]]. 

She was a former researcher with the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]], the [[SRI International|Stanford Research Institute]], and [[NASA]].<ref>[[Kit Pedler|Pedler, Kit]]. ''Mind Over Matter''. Taylor & Francis, 1981, p. 48.</ref>

In 1975 Rauscher co-founded the Berkeley [[Fundamental Fysiks Group]], an informal group of physicists who met weekly to discuss [[quantum mysticism]] and the philosophy of [[quantum physics]]. [[David Kaiser (physicist)|David Kaiser]] argued in his book, ''[[How the Hippies Saved Physics]]'' that this group helped to nurture ideas which were unpopular at the time within the physics community, but which later, in part, formed the basis of [[quantum information science]].<ref name=Kaiserxv>
[[David Kaiser (physicist)|Kaiser, David]]. ''How the Hippies Saved Physics: Science, Counterculture and the Quantum Revival''. W. W. Norton & Company, 2011, p. xv–xvii.
*Also see Kaiser, David. [http://forum-network.org/lectures/how-hippies-saved-physics "Lecture: How the Hippies Saved Physics"], WGBH PBS, April 28, 2010, from 38:00 mins.
*[[Gary Zukav|Zukav, Gary]]. ''[[The Dancing Wu Li Masters|The Dancing Wu Li Masters: An Overview of the New Physics]]''. HarperOne, 2001 (first published 1979), p. x.</ref>

Rauscher had an interest in [[psychic healing]] and [[faith healing]] and other [[paranormal]] claims.

==Early life, education and career==
Rauscher was born in Berkeley, California on March 18, 1937.<ref name=":0" />

In ''How the Hippies Saved Physics'' (2011), Kaiser writes that Rauscher had always been interested in science, and as a child had designed and built her own telescopes. Raised near Berkeley, she started hanging around the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory when she was in high school. She enrolled at Berkeley for her first degree, and published her first article, on nuclear fusion, while still an undergraduate. Kaiser writes that she was the only woman in her class; at that time women in America earned only five and two percent of physics undergraduate degrees and PhDs respectively. He writes that she coped with it by wearing tweedy dresses and keeping her hair short, though she experienced some intimidation. She obtained her master's in nuclear physics in 1965.<ref name=Kaiser49>Kaiser 2011, pp. 49–51.</ref> From 1975 to 1978, she was a researcher at the [[SRI International|Stanford Research Institute]]'s Radio Physics Laboratory.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://unifiedfieldtheories.com/about_us|title=About Us|publisher=BioHarmonic Resonance|accessdate=2012-03-02}}</ref>

She married and had a son, and when she became their sole provider took a job as a staff scientist at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. When her son was old enough, she returned to Berkeley to begin her PhD under [[Glenn Seaborg]], the nuclear chemist. She continued by working at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) and additionally started and chaired the Livermore Philosophy Group, offering classes on the relationship between science and society at Berkeley, and later at the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]].<ref name=Kaiser49/> She completed her PhD in 1978 on "Coupled Channel Alpha Decay Theory for Even and Odd-Mass Light and Heavy Nuclei."<ref>Rauscher, Elizabeth. [http://escholarship.org/uc/item/3t9674cg  "Coupled Channel Alpha Decay Theory for Even and Odd-Mass Light and Heavy Nuclei"], Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, February 1978.</ref>

She later held positions as professor of physics and general science at [[John F. Kennedy University]], 1978–1984; research consultant to [[NASA]], 1983–1985; and professor and graduate student adviser in the department of physics at the [[University of Nevada, Reno]], 1990–1998.<ref name="ERB">{{cite web|url=http://www.theresonanceproject.org/pdf/rauscher_cv_12_30_2008.pdf |title=Elizabeth A. Rauscher, Ph.D. Biography |accessdate=2011-12-03 |work=theresonanceproject.org |publisher=The Resonance Project |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20111019025909/http://www.theresonanceproject.org/pdf/rauscher_cv_12_30_2008.pdf |archivedate=2011-10-19 }}</ref><ref>[http://www.breakthru-technologies.com/presenters.html "Presenters: Elizabeth A. Rauscher, Ph.D."] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110903012731/http://www.breakthru-technologies.com/presenters.html |date=2011-09-03 }}, Breakthru-Technologies.com, accessed August 20, 2011.</ref>

==Fundamental Fysiks Group==
{{further|Fundamental Fysiks Group}}
{{external media
| float  = right
| width  = 240px
| image1 = [http://technoccult.net/wp-content/uploads/2010/06/Jack-Sarfatti.jpg Members of the Fundamental Fysiks Group], featured in [[Francis Ford Coppola]]'s ''City Magazine'' in 1975.<br>Left to right: [[Jack Sarfatti]], Saul-Paul Sirag, [[Nick Herbert (physicist)|Nick Herbert]], and (seated) [[Fred Alan Wolf]].
}}
At Berkeley in May 1975, she and George Weissmann co-founded the Fundamental Fysiks Group, an informal group of physicists who met for Friday afternoon brainstorming sessions to explore the philosophical problems posed by quantum physics, particularly the relationship between physics and [[consciousness]]. She named and chaired this group. The group included [[Fritjof Capra]], [[John Clauser]], [[Nick Herbert (physicist)|Nick Herbert]], [[Jack Sarfatti]], [[Henry Stapp]], and [[Fred Alan Wolf]]. According to Kaiser, Rauscher and Weissman started the meetings in a fit of pique and frustration, saddened by the absence of a philosophical perspective in their physics classes.<ref name=Kaiserxv/>

==Parapsychology==
Rauscher had an interest in [[psychic healing]] and [[faith healing]].<ref>*For psychic healing, see Smith, Jerry E. [https://books.google.com/books?id=G7t260XD8AYC&pg=PA79 ''Weather Warfare''], Adventures Unlimited Press, 2006, p. 79.
*For faith healing, see [[Dossey, Larry]]. [https://books.google.com/books?id=mXRDdKciVbsC&pg=PA147 ''Healing words: The power of prayer and the practice of medicine''], HarperCollins, 1993, p. 147.
*For remote viewing, see Jones, Marie D. [https://books.google.com/books?id=tVULQHPWnesC&pg=PA206 ''PSIence: How New Discoveries in Quantum Physics and New Science May Explain the Existence of Paranormal Phenomena''], Career Press, 2006, p. 206.</ref>

Kaiser describes how Rauscher's personal interests within the group lay with [[remote viewing]], [[precognition]], [[psychokinesis]], remote healing, and [[ghost]]s.<ref>Kaiser 2011, p. 262.</ref> [[Jeffrey John Kripal]] writes that Rauscher broadened the group to include non-physicists, and in the late 1970s and early 1980s the group's members met annually at the [[Esalen Institute]] to continue their exchange of ideas, exerting a major influence on alternative religious thought in the United States.<ref>[[Jeffrey J. Kripal|Kripal, Jeffrey John]]. [https://books.google.com/books?id=fzSP6BRFBzIC&pg=PA309 ''Esalen: America and the religion of no religion'']. University of Chicago Press, 2007, p. 309.</ref>

==Later research==
Starting in the early 1980s with her husband—William van Bise, an engineer—she researched the effects of electromagnetic fields on biological systems to enhance health. In the 1990s, Rauscher and van Bise, moved to an estate in [[Devotion, North Carolina]], owned by Richard J. Reynolds III, grandson of [[R. J. Reynolds]], the tobacco magnate. Until his death in 1994, Reynolds allowed them to live there to conduct research into the effects of electromagnetic fields on brain waves. A third scientist, physician [[Andrija Puharich]], had been living and conducting research on the estate since 1980. After Reynolds' death,  the scientists said he had invited them to remain there as long as they wanted, but they were unable to produce a written agreement.<ref>[http://nl.newsbank.com/nl-search/we/Archives?p_product=CO&s_site=charlotte&p_multi=CO&p_theme=realcities&p_action=search&p_maxdocs=200&p_topdoc=1&p_text_direct-0=0EB6CD2075B8409A&p_field_direct-0=document_id&p_perpage=10&p_sort=YMD_date:D&s_trackval=GooglePM "Scientists being asked to leave Reynolds estate"], ''The Charlotte Observer'', November 7, 1994.
*[https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=jHJAAAAAIBAJ&sjid=wlYMAAAAIBAJ&pg=4656,1467452&dq=william-van-bise&hl=en "Scientists sue for compensation after getting booted from estate"], ''The Robesonian'', November 7, 1994.
*[https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=bLQsAAAAIBAJ&sjid=KBUEAAAAIBAJ&pg=3993,66273&dq=elizabeth+rauscher&hl=en "Scientists ordered off estate of tobacco heir"], Associated Press, December 1, 1994.
*[http://nl.newsbank.com/nl-search/we/Archives?p_product=CO&s_site=charlotte&p_multi=CO&p_theme=realcities&p_action=search&p_maxdocs=200&p_topdoc=1&p_text_direct-0=0EB6CD70C5B9FAF8&p_field_direct-0=document_id&p_perpage=10&p_sort=YMD_date:D&s_trackval=GooglePM "The millionaire and the mad scientists"], ''The Charlotte Observer'', January 15, 1995.</ref>

== Death ==
Rauscher died on July 3, 2019, aged 82.<ref name=":0" />
